document.title: Memorandum of Conversation: Secretary's First One-on-One with Shevardnadze, March 21, 1988
document.authors: U.S. Department of State (Dennis Ross Collection, Reagan Library)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Withdrawal from Afghanistan 1989 | National Security Archive
document.note: Final ministerial before the Geneva Accords signing. Shevardnadze urges Shultz to limit US support for radical resistance forces, noting Gulbuddin Hekmatyar's election as Peshawar alliance leader and calling him 'a fundamentalist, a person of extreme views'. Shultz insists on 'symmetry'. Shevardnadze proposes a 'third option' dropping the arms-supply issue, and talks pass to deputies Adamishin and Armacost.

mentions.quote: THE SECRETARY welcomed Shevardnadze, noting that the two were meeting frequently.
SHEVARDNADZE said that what he had told the Secretary in his private office remained in effect. The Soviets had decided to withdraw.
POWELL noted that the U.S. was working hard to design JVE's which would meet our needs
Gorbachev had initially indicated it would be ten months; in Geneva they had agreed it could be nine.
The President was looking forward to seeing Shevardnaze on Wednesday

events.description: Shultz–Shevardnadze one-on-one discussing Afghanistan, Geneva accords, arms supply symmetry, Durand Line.
Shevardnadze told Shultz in the fall that Moscow had decided to withdraw from Afghanistan.
Hekmatyar elected leader of the Peshawar Alliance.
Planned follow-up meeting at 8:30 and expert-level talks (Armacost with Adamishin/Alekseev).
Shultz's first one-on-one with Shevardnadze in the Secretary's Outer Office covering ABM Treaty, nuclear testing, Afghanistan, Central America.
Planned meeting of President Reagan with Shevardnadze on Wednesday.
Previous fall: Shevardnadze told Shultz in his private office that Moscow had decided to withdraw from Afghanistan.
Soviets broke linkage between withdrawal and establishment of interim government.
At Geneva the Soviets agreed the withdrawal timetable could be nine months rather than ten.
Hekmatyar elected leader of the Peshawar Alliance.
Soviet troops withdrawn from twelve, now thirteen or fourteen, provinces of Afghanistan.
Shultz–Shevardnadze one-on-one discussing Afghan arms supply options (end US supply, US not guarantor, omit issue) and Geneva accords.
Planned follow-up meeting at 8:30 and expert working group (Armacost with Adamishin and Alekseev) to draft balanced formulation on arms supply.
Afghanistan began withholding recognition of the Durand Line.
Shultz states U.S. would supply those it aided if the USSR supplied its clients, and humanitarian aid would continue.

key_claims: Shevardnadze confirmed the USSR would withdraw within nine months, half of forces in the first three months, completed by year-end 1988.
The Soviets broke the linkage between withdrawal and an interim government in Kabul.
Shevardnadze said Hekmatyar's election as Peshawar Alliance leader complicated prospects for a coalition and warned he might move camps to Iran.
The USSR refused to cut arms to the Kabul regime; the U.S. insisted on symmetry as guarantor, with Shultz favoring leaving arms supply out of the accords (third option).
Shevardnadze called U.S. aid to anti-government forces illegal and said ideally the U.S. would stop supplying Hekmatyar.
The Durand Line wording ('internationally recognized border' vs 'existing borders') was the last obstacle to signing at Geneva.
